en: The First Chapter: Now, the Enumeration of Phonemes (Varṇasamāmnāya). 1. Now, from the beginning, there are the homogeneous vowels (*samānākṣara*). 2. Two by two, they consist of short and long phonemes of the same class (*savarṇa*). 3. A protracted (*pluta*) vowel is not [homogeneous] with what precedes it. 4. From the beginning, sixteen are the vowels (*svara*). 5. The remainder are the consonants (*vyañjana*). 6. The first twenty-five are the stops (*sparśa*). 7. The following four are the semivowels (*antasthā*). 8. The final six are the sibilants (*ūṣman*). 9. Of the stops, there are five groups (*varga*) in successive order. 10. These are: first, second, third, fourth, and last. 11. Among the sibilants, the *visarjanīya*, and the first and second [stops], those without voice (*aghoṣa*) are [unaspirated]. 12. The letter *ha* is not [so]. 13. [End.]

14. That which has a consonant remaining [is called] *ghoṣavat*. 15. *Ā*, *pra*, *upa*, *abhi*, *adhi*, *prati*, *pari*, and *vi* are prefixes (*upasarga*). 16. A phoneme followed by the letter *ka* is designated as "the letter" (*varṇākhyā*). 17. Among consonants, [the name of the preceding letter applies] when separated by the vowel *a*. 18. This does not apply to the *visarjanīya*, *jihvāmūlīya*, *upadhmānīya*, *anusvāra*, or *nāsikya*. 19. But for the letter *ra*, it is [the name of the following letter] *e* or *pha*. 20. A short vowel followed by a letter is the name of the three [preceding sounds]. 21. The vowel *a* [is the name] of consonants. 22. [The same applies] to that which is being grasped [as a technical term]. 23. The letter *aḥ* [is the name] of those [elements] that undergo augmentation (*āgama*), modification (*vikārin*), or elision (*lopin*). 24. Or rather, there is the grasping [of the intended meaning]. 25. In case of doubt, [the rule applies to] that which is proximate. 26. [This applies] even to multiple [sounds].

The first [of the vowels] is *vargottara*; the designation of the *vargas* is 27; the modification (*vikāra*) is 28; "prior" (*pūrva*) means the preceding [consonant] 29; "subsequent" (*para*) means the following [consonant] 30; the short vowels are *ṛ* and *ḷ* 31; and the vowel *a* 32; by that [measure], a vowel of equal duration [is long] 33; the *anusvāra* is also [of equal duration] 34; the long vowel is twice that [duration] 35; the protracted (*pluta*) is three times [that] 36; a consonant has half the duration of a short vowel 37; high-pitched is the acute (*udātta*) 38; low-pitched is the grave (*anudātta*) 39; the combination [of these two] is the circumflex (*svarita*) 40; its beginning is higher than the acute, for as much as half the duration of a short vowel, provided there is an interval [between the accents] 41.

42. The remainder is like the acute (udātta). 43. Even when accompanied by a consonant. 44. Or, if not separated [by another vowel], it may be lower than that. 45. Or, it is like the grave (anudātta). 46. Its beginning is like the acute; the remainder is like the grave—so say the teachers. 47. Some say the whole [word] is inclined [toward the grave]. 48. It should be treated as if it were separate words when there is no counting [of syllables]. 49. Of that, the preceding word is the avagraha. 50. In the case of word-utterances, the word should be understood. 51. Even when modified. 52. Also when beginning with the letter *a*. 53. And also when beginning with the letter *aṅ*. 54. A single phoneme is a word when uncombined (*apṛkta*). 55. It is treated like the beginning or the end. 56. Of a phoneme.

56. Elision and modification [are governed by the following rules]. 57. Destruction is elision (*lopa*). 85. Subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*) applies to the final [syllable]. 59. However, a suffixal marker (*upabandha*) always serves to indicate location. 60. And that which belongs to different words is the cause for *pragraha* and so forth in the case of *srādi* and similar forms. 61. That which has been stated is repeated starting from three words; starting from three words. Thus ends the first chapter. The second chapter begins.

Now, concerning the production of sound: (1) from the impelling of the body-wind upon the junction of the throat and chest, (2) its resonances (*prātiśrutkāni*) arise; [namely] the chest, throat, head, mouth, and nostrils. (3) When the throat is constricted, *nāda* (resonance) is produced; (4) when it is opened, *śvāsa* (breath); (5) in between, the *hakāra* (the sound *ha*). (6) These are the primary sources of the phonemes (*varṇaprakṛti*). (7) *Nāda* is the secondary emission (*anupradāna*) in the case of vowels and voiced consonants; (8) *hakāra* is the secondary emission for the fourth letters of the *ha*-class; (9) *śvāsa* is the secondary emission for the unvoiced consonants; (10) it is more abundant in the others than in the first [classes]; (11) in the vowel *a*, the lips and jaws are not excessively drawn together.

12. It is not excessively spread apart. 13. And for the vowel *o*, the lips are more closely drawn together. 14. For the vowel *e*, they are slightly protruded. 15. The jaws are more closely drawn together. 16. One touches the upper teeth with both the middle and the tip of the tongue. 17. And for the vowels *ṛ*, *ṝ*, and *ḷ*—which are short (*barsva*)—one draws them closer together. 18. According to some, this also applies to the anusvāra and the vowels that follow it. 19. In the absence of a specific instruction, the tongue is extended forward. 20. The lips are as in the case of the vowel *a*. 21. The tongue is placed against the palate for the vowel *i*. 22. And likewise for the vowel *e*. 23. [And for the vowel *ai*.]

The closing of the lips occurs in the vowel *u* (24). But everywhere else, [the modification] is one interval away from the original [organ] (25). Half of the vowel *a* is the beginning of the vowels *e* and *o* (26). According to some, it is closer than the closed articulation (27). The vowel *i* is one and a half [moras]; it is the remainder of the preceding [vowel] (28). The vowel *u*, however, belongs to the following [vowel] (29). The nasals (*anusvāra*) and the last [consonants of each class] are nasalized (*anunāsika*) (30). That place where the vowels are brought together is the place of articulation (*sthāna*) (31). That which brings them together is the instrument (*karaṇa*) (32). According to others, however, that where there is contact is the place of articulation (33); that by which one makes contact is the instrument (34).

35. One touches the root of the palate with the root of the tongue at the root of the jaw for the *ka*-group (*sparśa*). 36. With the middle of the tongue at the palate for the *ca*-group. 37. Having encircled [the tip] with the tip of the tongue at the head for the *ṭa*-group. 38. With the tip of the tongue at the roots of the teeth for the *ta*-group. 39. With both lips for the *pa*-group. 40. At the palate with the middle and the end of the tongue for the letter *ya*. 41. With the middle of the tip of the tongue against the inner roots of the teeth for the letter *ra*. 42. And at the roots of the teeth for the letter *la*. 43. With the ends of the lips and the teeth for the letter *va*. 44. The sibilants (*ūṣman*) are produced in their respective order at the places of articulation of the *sparśas*.

The middle of the consonants (*karaṇa*) is open (45). The letters *ha* and *visarjanīya* have the throat as their place of articulation (*sthāna*) (46). According to some, *ha* has the same place of articulation as the following vowel (47). *Visarjanīya* has the same place of articulation as the preceding letter (48). The *nāsikya* sounds have the nose as their place of articulation (49), or they may be articulated by both the mouth and the nose (50). In these cases, they are treated like the [nasalized] series (*varga*) (51). Nasality (*ānunāsikya*) arises from the opening of the nasal passage; nasality arises from the opening of the nasal passage (52). Thus ends the second chapter. The third chapter begins.

Now begins the third chapter. Now, first, in the northern division, a short vowel followed by a consonant [is pluta]: 1. *devāśīkā-sumnāśva-rtāvayunā-hṛdayā-ghā-ukthā-śuddhā*; 2. *indrā-vadvanvān paraḥ*; 3. *citrā va-paraḥ*; 4. *prasthendriyā-draviṇā-viśvadevyā-dīrghāvīryā-viśvāvātā-tvā-bhaṅgurā-karṇakā-vṛṣṇiyā-sugopa-arka-sāmā-ghā-satrā-varṣā-puṣpā-meghā-prāsvā*; 5. *loka-eveṣṭā*; 6. *śakti-rathī-tviṣīvā-śīrā-tryoṣadhyā-hutī*.

*vyāhṛtīḥ*, *svāhākṛtīḥ*, *hrādunīḥ*, *śacīcitīḥ*, *śroṇī*, *puṣṭī*, *pūti*, *abhicarṣaṇī*, *paryadhī*, *pārīśatrū*, *viṣūvasū*, *anūhanūsū*, *vibhū*—this is the *avagraha*. *ava*, *asacasva*, *anu*, *adāmṛḍa*, *avardha*, *aśikṣa*, *arakṣa*, *adya*, *abha*, *vābhaja*, *ya*, *trā*, *cara*, *piba*, *anādhāma*, *adhāraya*, *adharṣa*, *aghā*, *avardhaya*, *abodha*, *atra*, *atra*, *amuñca*, *aśvasya*, *apuṇaḥ*, *svāhiṣṭha*, *atvam*, *arājan*, *niṣva*, *yakṣva*, *achā*. *atha agni yājye*. *kutra adakṣiṇena asvena āha*.

*antana-ājagāma-āruha-imā-avidma-ardhyām-ācakṛma-akṣāmā-astarīmā-bharemā-varṣayatha-irayatha-arithā-pātha-athā-siñcata-ajanayata-jayatā-akṣatā-vatā-yātā-aśṛṇuta-akṛṇuta-abibhrta 10 bharata yā jyāsu 11 atta-abhavata-anadata-atarata-atapatā-ajuhuta-avocatā-amuñcata-acṛta-aghṛṣya-ajanaya-vartaya-āsādaya-apāraya-adīya-hara-bhaga-pā-samādā-sūja-tiṣṭha-ayena 12 uśmasi-kriyī kṛdhi-śrudhi-yadi 13 sūtūnū-mithū-makṣū-ū 14 vyutpūrva ānanudātto 'nūṣmavaty-anūṣmavati 15. Thus ends the third chapter.

The Fourth Chapter. Now begins the Fourth Chapter. Now, regarding the *pragrahas* (words that remain unelided): 1. [The following words are *pragrahas*: *nau*, *avagrahāḥ*, *antāḥ*, *iti* even when followed by another word (*parah*), the vowel *ū*, the vowel *o* when not joined in *saṃhitā* (*asāṃhitaḥ*) and followed by the vowel *a* or a consonant, and the words preceded by *sam*, *mahat*, *atha*, *pit*. 2. Furthermore, the vowels *e* and *ai* [are *pragrahas*] when they are not joined in *saṃhitā* and followed by the vowel *a* or a consonant. 3. Also, the words *asme*, *tve* ending in a nasal (*aniṅgyāntaḥ*), and the following: *devate*, *ubhe*, *bhārādhe*, *ūrdhve*, *viśākhe*, *pravṛṅge*, *ene*, *medhye*, *tṛṇṇe*, *tṛdye*, *kanīnike*, *pārśve*, *śive*, *cottame*, *evottare*, *śipre*, and *rathaṃtare*.

O you two who are the forms of the year—O you of diverse forms, O you of manifold forms, O you who possess abundant sacrificial food, O you who are the pressing-stones, O day and night, O you whose vow is clarified butter, O hymn and liturgy, O Ṛg and Sāman, O you who are manifest and established, O you who belong to the Raivata [Sāman], O you who are fulfilled, O you who are offered, O you who are separated, O you who are true, O you who are flawless, O you who are abundant, O you who are born of old—prepare the seat. These two eyes, the two black ones, the two deities Phalgunī, the two fists, the two intellects, the two naves, the two omentum-roasting spits, the two days, the two births, the two auspicious ones, the two Sāmans, the two belonging to Viṣṇu, the two made of sugarcane.

The two ladles; heaven and earth (12); and the former (13); he does not obstruct eternally (14); the two offerings, the golden ones, the victorious ones, the well-offered ones, the fashioning ones, the speckled ones (15); and the former (16); the two garments, the two heats, the two worlds (17); and the latter (18); with the expansive ones, the longing ones, the earth (19); those two which have spread out wide, those two of this [world], the two roaring ones, the metrical ones, those two moving between these (20); not in the lap (21); the nourishing one, beginning with "the support" (22); "O first-born, through the support" (23); these two.

*garbham upa-ivarasena paraḥ* (24); *krūram āpaḥ sa-jūr brahma-jait-eṣu ca* (25); *pūrṇe* (26); *dṛḍhe* (27); *ghnī-cakre pa-pare* (28); *nv-atī* (29); *pa-paro na* (30); *samīcī* (31); *na-paro na* (32); *cī yat pra-paraḥ* (33); *ān mahī* (34); *patī śrutiḥ* (35); *gnī* (36); *na hi-paraḥ* (37); *vīḍ-dvārau kṛṣṇaś carāvo yadā paraḥ* (38); *na jñe 'hne nityam* (39); but when preceded by the vowels *ā* or *e*, in the case of a polysyllabic word, [the rule applies] to those two (*te*) (40); *na śāryate* (41); *te*.

Do not let the wind blow upon this [fetus]; may another [wind] carry it away. (42) The *anudātta* [vowel] is not always [so]. (43) These two bodies are indeed equal, for they are taught as bricks in the sacrificial path. (44) And the subsequent [syllable] is [long] in both cases. (45) The word *sthaḥ* is subsequent. (46) And the subsequent [syllable] is [long] in both cases. (47) For Soma, in this [case]. (48)

Two [syllables] 49; and when followed by another [word], even if separated by one or two [syllables] 51, [the *pluti* occurs] when they cause [the sense] to go, when they signify existence, after the syllable *anū*, when [the verb] means "he made thin," "he would make," or "he makes" in the context of sacrifices (*iṣṭi*), when [the verbs] mean "they spoke," "may they proceed," "may they support," or "he causes to recite," when [the phrase] means "they maintain Agni," or when it is *gāyatram*; by both of these [conditions], up to the sixth [chapter], there is the intermediate [rule] 52. Not in the village, nor in the case of *varcas*, nor in the case of a couple, nor in this world does he place [it] 53. Always when on the same word, and in *ave* and *cāve* 54. Thus ends the fourth chapter. The fifth chapter begins.

Now begins the fifth chapter. Now, regarding the *saṃhitā* (phonetic combination) when there is a single breath (*ekaprāṇabhāva*): 1. The rule as it has been prescribed is its original form (*sāprakṛti*). 2. In that regard, each preceding [rule] is the first. 3. A *śakara* [consonant] preceded by *trapu* or *mithu* [becomes a sibilant]. 4. And one preceded by *su* [becomes a sibilant] when followed by *candra*. 5. A *sakāra* preceded by *sa* [becomes a sibilant] when followed by *kuru*. 6. And when followed by a suffix (*pratyaya*) that does not begin with *k* [it becomes a sibilant]. 7. A *dakāra* preceded by a low-pitched vowel (*nīcāpūrva*) and followed by a high-pitched vowel (*uccāpara*) [becomes a sibilant]. 8. An *arakāra* preceded by *asaṃ* [becomes a sibilant]. 9. In the *avagraha*, for the words *āśīḥ*, *dhūḥ*, and *suvar*, the following *sakāra* becomes a *ṣakāra*. 10. Now...

11. Elision [occurs]. 12. A *m* preceded by *īṃ*. 13. A *v* preceded by *tu* or *nu*, when followed by two acute-accented vowels. 14. An *s* preceded by *ut*, when followed by a consonant. 15. And [the rule] "of *eṣas* and *sa*" [also applies]. 16. Not [so] for *nāsaḥ*. 17. When followed by *id*, *vid*, *agnaiḥ*, *imām*, *na*, *enaḥ*, or *oṣadhīḥ*, an *s* [becomes *ṣ*]. 18. The term "avagraha" [is used] as a single unit. 19. [The word] "tiṣṭhanti" with its preceding [word], when followed by one [vowel]. 20. A *n* [becomes *ṇ*] when followed by a *ś*. 21. [The words] *nāyan*, *nairayan*, *nāndhruvan*, *anaḍvān*, *ghṛṇīvān*, *vāruṇān*, and *evāsmin* [are treated similarly]. 22. A *t* [becomes *ṇ*] when followed by *k*, *ś*, *c*, or *ch*. 23. When followed by *j*, it becomes *j*. 24. [And] a *n*.

24. In these [rules], when followed by *l*, the nasal *ñ* becomes *l*. 25. When followed by *n*, the nasal *n* becomes *l*. 26. A nasalized *n* [is produced] when followed by a nasal (*anunāsika*). 27. When followed by a stop (*sparśa*), the nasal *m* becomes a nasalized sound corresponding to the place of articulation (*sthāna*) of that stop. 28. And when followed by a semivowel (*antasthā*), it becomes a nasalized sound homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with it. 29. It does not become so when followed by the letter *r*. 30. According to some teachers, it does not become so when followed by *y* or *v*. 31. Ātreya says that because of the absence of the final [nasal], the preceding [consonant] becomes nasalized. 32. The letter *k* preceded by *ṅ* and followed by *ṣ* or *s* [becomes *kh*]. 33. And the letter *t* preceded by *ṭ* or *n* [becomes *th*]. 34. The letter *ś* preceded by a stop (*sparśa*) becomes *ch*. 35. It does not become so when preceded by *m*.

35. According to Vālmīki, [the letter *pa*] preceded by *ka* [is nasalized]. 36. According to Pauṣkarasādi, it is nasalized when followed by a consonant, but not when preceded by one; nor is the letter *ña* [nasalized] in that case. 37. According to Plākṣi, Kauyiḍinya, Gautama, and Pauṣkarasādi, the letter *ha* preceded by the first [surd] is replaced by its fourth [nasal], which shares the same place of articulation (*sthāna*). 38. According to some, it remains unchanged. 39. According to Śaityāyana and others, the fourth [nasal] occurs in the interval. 40. And according to the Mīmāṃsakas, and again according to the Mīmāṃsakas. 41. Thus ends the fifth chapter; now the sixth chapter.

Now begins the sixth chapter. Now, regarding the letter *ṣa*, [the following rules apply to] the letters *sa* and *visarjanīya*: 1. [The *ṣatva* substitute occurs] in the words *svānāso divyāpo haṃyamuka mūmoprotrīmahidya vipadyava yaha*, when preceded by [the aforementioned conditions]. 2. In the words *asadāmāsiñcaśca*. 3. When preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*) or the word *niṣ*, provided the following word is unaccented (*anudātta*). 4. In the words *rāsaḥ sapte agninirvidurnīḍhuḥ pāyubhirveḥ sumatirmākirīyurāyurābhiḥ sadhirna*, it is always [the case] when followed by the letter *ta*. 5. Now, [there are exceptions]: 6. [The *ṣatva* substitute does not occur] when preceded by a vowel (*avarṇa*), a consonant (*vyañjana*), or the words *śakuni*, *patnī*, *ṛtu*, *mṛtyu*, *malimlu*, or *bṛhaspati*. 7. [End of section.]

8. [The word] containing *dhakāra* or *repha* [is not elided]; 9. the *avagraha*; 10. [the word] having its own place; 11. [this rule does not apply] when preceded by *dhi*; 12. after [words ending in] *sat*, *tāna*, *ebhyaḥ*, *sapta*, *abhiḥ*, *saṃmitān*, *tanūm*, *asitaṃ*, *spaśaḥ*, *sak*, *sanisaniḥ*, *sanīḥ*, *sabheyaḥ*, *sattvā*, *sasyāyai*; 13. [the word] *na* [is not elided] when followed by *svar*, *spardhāḥ*, *tarīm*, *asāhasra*, *sārathi*, *sphurantī*, *stubh*, *jyotiḥ*, *āyuḥ*, or a word beginning with *catur*. [The following words are not elided: *tahān*, *tasmin*, *lokān*, *vidvān*, *tān*, *trīn*, *yuṣmān*, *ūrdhvān*, *ambakān*, *ṛtūn*.
*śmankṛṇvan*, *pitṝnanān*, *kapālāṃstiṣṭhan*, *nādyudāttenemirdevāntsavane*, *paśūstakāraparaḥ sakāram*, *prākṛto nitye*, *prākṛto nitye*. Thus ends the sixth chapter;
[now] the seventh chapter.

Now begins the seventh chapter. Now, the letter *na* [becomes *ṇa*] when preceded by *ṣu*, *sūkṛ*, *dhi*, *suvaḥ*, *sam*, *indra*, *asthūri*, *uru*, *vāḥ*, *ṣaṭ*, *tri*, *grāma*, *niṣu*, or a word beginning with *ni*. (1) It also becomes *ṇa* when followed by the root *han* (*hanyāt*) or the participle *upyamāna*. (2) [The *na* of *pari* becomes *ṇa*] when preceded by *pari-pari*, *pari*, or *pra*. (3) This occurs even when an *a*-vowel intervenes. (4) Also in *vāhana*, *ūhyamāna*, *yāna*, *ayana*, *avena*, and *avaṃśca*. (5) And when preceded by *prā*. (6) In *indra*, it does not become *ṇa* when preceded by a word ending in *yajus* or by *enaṃ kena*. (7) In *nṛśrī*, it does not become *ṇa* when preceded by *manāḥ*. (8) In *aṅgānām*, *one*, *egāni*, *gānām*, *gyāni*, and *yāmena*, [the *na* remains *na*]. (9) When preceded by *ra* or *ṣa*, [the *na* of] *havani*, *ahlai*, and *han* [remains *na*]. (10) When preceded by *ru*, [the *na* of] *mayāni* and *anī* [remains *na*]. (11)

The *vāghāṣa* [sandhi] preceded by *taṣṭam* 13; and *tha* followed by *ṭha* 14; [the sandhi] where *na* is followed by the letter *ta* 15; "for indeed, they surely dance with one another, each with the other, both within and without" 16. Thus ends the seventh chapter. The eighth chapter.

Now begins the eighth chapter; now the first [section]. 1. When followed by an *uttama* (voiced) consonant, it becomes an *uttama* (voiced) sibilant (*savargīya*). 2. In the third [chapter], when followed by a vowel (*svara*) or a sonant (*ghoṣavat*) consonant. 3. *Ka*, *ku*, and *ca* when followed by the letter *m*. 4. Now, regarding the *visarjanīya* (the visarga). 5. Among these [consonants], it becomes a *repha* (the letter *r*). 6. It does not become a *repha* when followed by [another] *repha*. 7. [The following words retain their *visarjanīya*: *hlāra-bhāḥ*, *rvāhā-ra-bi-bha-ra-jī-ga-ra-ka-ra-anantara-vivaḥ-suvaḥ-punar-ahaḥ-ahaḥ-prātaḥ-vastaḥ-śamitaḥ-samitaḥ-sanuta-stanuta-stotara-hotara-pitara-mātara-aṣṭara-iṣṭara-neṣṭara-tvaṣṭara*. 8. *Ka-ra-va-ra* in an unaccented (*anudātta*) word. 9. *Antara-* [retains its *visarjanīya*].

10. [The *visarga*] is not elided before a vowel that is acutely accented (*udātta*). 11. It is not elided when followed by *āvṛt*. 12. Nor when followed by *iti*. 13. Also not when followed by *ahar-ahaḥ*, *suvar*, or words ending in *agni* and *gī*. 14. Nor when followed by *bhis* or *bhyām*. 15. And [the *visarga*] of all [words] is not elided before *aṃhas*. 16. However, when preceded by a non-vowel (*anavarṇa*) and followed by *repha* (*r*), it is elided. 17. And the preceding [vowel] becomes long. 18. And [the *visarga*] of *eṣṭa* [is elided]. 19. Not according to some teachers. 20. According to others, both [the *visarga* and the preceding vowel] of the word *uttarīya* become *repha*. 21. According to Sāṃkṛtya, [only] the *ukāra* [becomes *repha*]. 22. According to Ukhya, [only the *ukāra*] together with the preceding [vowel] [becomes *repha*]. 23. A *samavagraha* occurs when *ṣa* is preceded by *s* and followed by *ka*, *kha*, or *pa*.

24. *āvirniriḍaḥ* (from *āvis-nir-iḍas*), *śaśvato'paso* (from *śaśvataḥ-apasaḥ*), *devariṣoṃ'haso'ti* (from *deva-riṣas-aṃhasas-ati*), *divoviśvato'śmanastamasaḥ* (from *divas-viśvatas-aśmanaḥ-tamasaḥ*). 25. *kṛdhipinvapatheparaḥ*. 26. *na sakraghakārapare*. 27. *patnīvepatī-patepatayepatiṣpatiṃparaḥ*. 28. *divaḥsahasaspariputparaḥ*. 29. *rāyaspoparaḥ*. 30. *namaskaroparaḥ*. 31. *vasuṣkakāraparaḥ*. 32. *nādhvaraṃviśvato'ntarjātoviviśuḥparuḥ punaḥ*. 33. *dhaṣavati*. 34. *parivāpraparaḥ*. 35. *na nirṇa niḥ*. Thus ends the eighth chapter. [The] ninth chapter.

Now begins the ninth chapter. 1. According to Kāṇḍamāyana, a sibilant (*ūṣman*) is elided when followed by another sibilant that is not voiced (*aghoṣa*). 2. For him, the sibilant is replaced by a corresponding stop (*saṃsthāna*) when followed by a voiced sound. 3. It is not elided when followed by *kṣ*. 4. Nor is it elided when followed by the *ka*-class or the *pa*-class, according to Agniveśya and Vālmīki. 5. According to some teachers, it is elided only when followed by a sibilant. 6. This does not apply in the opinion of Plākṣi and Plākṣāyaṇa. 7. Every *o* sound followed by an *a* sound is [treated as] *au*. 8. And [it remains so] when followed by a voiced sound (*ghoṣavat*). 9. But when preceded by an *a*-vowel, it is elided. 10. Now, when followed by a vowel (*svara*), it becomes *y*. 11. The *e* sound becomes *ay*. 12. The *o* sound becomes *av*. 13. Not when followed by an *ā* sound.

The vowel *ai* (aikāra) is *āyam* (14); the vowel *au* (aukāra) is *āvam* (15). An uncombined *u* (ukāro 'pṛktaḥ) remains in its original form (*prakṛtyā*), as does *va* when it occurs between [two vowels] (vakāro 'ntare) (16). A *saṃhitā* [sandhi] does not occur in such cases (na tattasmāt sāṃhitaḥ) (17). A *ṅ* preceded by a short vowel constitutes two syllables (hrasvapūrvo ṅakāro dvivarṇam) (18), as does a *n* (nakāraśca) (19). In the words *grahaḥ*, *khyāya*, *ājyā*, *pṛṣṭhya*, and *hiraṇyavarṇīya*, an *i* or *u* followed by *r* becomes *r*, and an *ā* followed by *r* becomes *y* (anitiparo graho khyayājyāpṛṣṭhyahiraṇyavarṇīyeṣv īkārokārapūrvo repham ākārapūrvaśca yakāram) (20).

May he who is preceded by Soma—immortal among mortals, difficult to approach—bring us cattle, honey, oblations, and those most worthy of invocation; may he, the knower of the seers, the possessor of praise, the lord of Kakṣīvat, the possessor of Bāṇa, the one rich in milk, the finder of barren cows, the finder of enemies, men, nourishments, and greatness. 21. O Indra, you have mounted these; let them come here to me. May the most excellent sacrificer come to my offerings. Let Aditi milk the lower ones first; may the enemy be powerless. 22. I shall not slacken the reins, nor the coursers, nor the birds;
I shall honor the equal ones, the most victorious. 23. And forth the other, and forth the other. 24. Thus ends the ninth chapter. The tenth chapter begins.

Now begins the tenth chapter. 1. Now, when *eka* (the vowel *e*) is followed by both [vowels], it becomes *aikāra*. 2. A long vowel remains unchanged when followed by a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) vowel. 3. Now, when preceded by *a*, [the following rules apply]. 4. When followed by an *i*-vowel, *eka* becomes *ekāra*. 5. When followed by an *u*-vowel, it becomes *okāra*. 6. When followed by *e* or *ai*, it becomes *aikāra*. 7. When followed by *o* or *au*, it becomes *aukāra*. 8. When followed by *a* or *ṛ*, it becomes *ara*. 9. When preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*), it becomes *āra*. 10. When followed by an acute-accented (*udātta*) vowel, it becomes acute-accented. 11. When followed by a nasalized (*anunāsika*) vowel, it becomes nasalized. 12. In the combination of a circumflex-accented (*svarita*) and an acute-accented (*anudātta*) vowel, it becomes circumflex-accented (*svarita*). 13. This does not occur in the words *dhāmā*, *pāsi*, *parībudhniya*, *ājyā*, *pūṣā*, *minanta*, and *ārṣe*.

In this [treatise], when *e* and *ai* follow *i* and *ī*, the latter are elided. (14) When *i* and *ī* are followed by *y* and *v*, they become *y* and *v*. (15) Furthermore, when two acute-accented vowels are followed by an unaccented vowel, it becomes circumflex (*svarita*). (16) And also when *ū* is substituted. (17) The pair *ś* and *y* are not [elided]. (18) However, *y* and *v* preceded by *a* are elided. (19) Not so for [the word] *ukhya*. (20) But according to Sāṃkṛtya, there is the substitution of *a*. (21) According to Mācākīya, those [sounds] followed by *u* and *ū* are elided. (22) According to Vātsapra, there is a trace (*leśa*) of these two. (23) This does not apply to protracted (*pluta*) or separated (*pragraha*) vowels. (24) And the following [rule applies] again and again. (25) Thus ends the tenth chapter. The eleventh chapter begins.

Now the eleventh chapter. 1. The letter *t* is elided when preceded by *e* or *o*. 2. Now follows the section on elision (*alopa*). 3. [The following words undergo elision: *dhātā*, *rātiḥ*, *upa*, *vājapeya-juṣṭa-*, *śyenāya*, *ukhya-*, *dhruva-kṣitiḥ*, *iyameva sā*, *agniḥ mūrdhā*, *rudra-prathama-upottama-vikarṣa-vihavya-hiṇya-varṇīya-yājyā-mahāpuṣṭhya*. 4. [Elision occurs] in *am̐haḥ*, *mogha-tiḥ*, *aniṣṭataḥ*, *avantu asmān*, *avadyāt*, and *ahani*. 5. [Elision occurs] in *anu gharma āpaḥ*, *marto rathaḥ*, *tvā adatte vātaḥ pūrvaḥ*. 6. [Elision occurs] in *abhivātu apaśca*. 7. [Elision occurs] in *anvagaman ca*.

8. *āpaḥ* is preceded by *addhi*, [and] *apāṃ napāt* [is preceded by *asmān*]. 9. *rāye* is preceded by *saindraḥ*, and *pūrvaḥ* is followed by *cākāra*. 10. *te* is preceded by *pūrvaḥ*, and *adya* [is preceded by] *gandhaḥ*; *aṃśuḥ* is at the beginning. 11. And *me* is preceded by [the same]. 12. *asya* [is preceded by *āśvinā*], and the subsequent [word] is *ca*. 13. *naḥ* is preceded by *pūrvaḥ*; *asad agniḥ* [is preceded by *aghāntamaḥ*]; *abhi* [occurs] in this [context] on the path today. 14. *namaḥ* is preceded by *pūrvaḥ*; *agne aśvebhyaḥ* [is preceded by *agni-yāya*]. 15. *ā* [is preceded by *vittaḥ*], *somaḥ* is preceded by *pūrvaḥ*, and is followed by *agniḥ*. 16. *dhīrāsaḥ adabdhāsaḥ ekādaśa asam ṛṣīṇām putraḥ śāryāte aṣāḍhaḥ pitāraḥ*.

Those who sit at the earth-sacrifice, whom I take [for you], O Agni—this one has been born for you; he is the nourisher, he who is upon your back, the lord, the vigorous bull, the son, the kindled one, the bull, the protector of the path, he who delights in the highest place, that Rudra, the first of the bulls. He who is the charioteer of this sacrifice, who hastens across, who passes beyond debts, who is free from disease, who desires food, whose flame is in the offerings, who is unconquered, who is without loss, who is great by day, the mother, the steed—Aṅgiras made him his own skin; he who is unshakable, the winner of horses, he who rests upon the bones, the inviolable one in the limbs. The sacrifice, the light, the further shore. He.
According to some, it is similar to the first half; according to others, it is similar to half [of the first]. 19 Thus ends the eleventh chapter.
The twelfth chapter begins.

Now begins the twelfth chapter. Now follows the section on elision (*lopa*). 1. *asi* (is elided). 2. *na garbhaḥ saṃnaddho'yamo bhadraḥ pūrvaḥ* (the word *na*, when preceded by *garbhaḥ*, *saṃnaddhaḥ*, *ayamaḥ*, or *bhadraḥ*, is elided). 3. *yavano'paraḥ svarapareṣu* (the word *yavanaḥ*, when followed by vowels, is elided). 4. *jakārāgnapara udāttaḥ* (an acute-accented vowel following *ja* or *agni* is elided). 5. *movacodadhānasthe pūrvaśca* (in the words *mo*, *vacas*, *dadhānaḥ*, and *sthe*, the preceding [vowel] is also elided). 6. *abhyāvartin napūpamapidhāmyadyānvaditihśarmāgnerjihvāmagnayaḥ paprayo'smākamasmeddhattāśmāśvāśrutiraśyāmāmāryamanasmatpāśānasminyajñe'stāvyathamānābhidrohamadhāyyado'tho'dugdhāriṣṭā* (in these phrases—*abhyāvartin*, *napūpam*, *apidhāmi adya*, *anvaditiḥ śarma agneḥ jihvām*, *agnayaḥ paprayaḥ asmākam*, *asmai dhatta aśmā aśvāḥ śrutiḥ aśyāma amā ariyam*, *anna asmat pāśān asmin yajñe*, *astā avyathamānā abhidroham adhāyi adaḥ*, *atha u adugdhā ariṣṭā*—the preceding [vowels] are elided).

The *aratha* verses sing within this [fire-altar], standing here; O Aṅgiras, you have performed the rite for us. 7. Being born, plunging in, considering himself a weapon, he falls from the trees; O self-dependent one, from the heat, from both sides, the measured fires, O Adhvaryu, have been prepared first. 8. When there is an unraised (*anudātta*) syllable before it, the raised (*udātta*) syllable becomes circumflex (*svarita*). 9. And when there is an unraised syllable before a raised one, it becomes raised. 10. And the circumflex is always [circumflex]; and the circumflex is always [circumflex]. 11. Thus ends the twelfth chapter. The thirteenth chapter.

Now begins the thirteenth chapter. Now, regarding the elision of the letter *m*: 1. [The *m* is elided] when followed by a *repha* (the letter *r*) or a sibilant (*ūṣman*). 2. According to some teachers, it is also [elided] when followed by the letter *y* or *v*. 3. In the case of the word *saṃsā*, the *m* is not elided when followed by *r*. 4. Now, concerning the phonemes (*varṇa*): 5. The letter *n* becomes *ṇ* within the same word (*samānapada*) when preceded by *ṛ*, *ṝ*, or the letter *ṣ*. 6. This also occurs even when [the preceding vowel] is separated [from the *ṇ* by other sounds]. 7. As in the word *hiraṇmayam*. 8. In the words *pāṇi*, *gaṇa*, *puṇyaka*, *kaṇva*, *kāṇa*, *gāṇa*, *cāṇava*, *veṇu*, *guṇa*, *maṇi*, and *pravāda*, the preceding [nasal] becomes *ṇ*. 9. Also in *paṇi*, *paṇim*, *vīyam*, *maṇa*, and *ūṇya*. 10. [The nasal becomes *ṇ*] when followed by the *ṭa*-class consonants (*ṭavarga*). 11. [The rule applies] when followed by [the *ṭa*-class].

*caṅkuṇa*, *phaṇat*, *sthūṇa*, *uhiṇu*, *yāddhiṇoti*, *kauṇeya*, *aṇiṣṭā*, *ulbaṇa*, *mugaṇa*, *śruti*, *cupuṇī*, *bāṇijāyā*, *aṇavaḥ*, *cāṇṇara*, *ārasthāṇum*, *tūṇavevīṇāyām*, *aśloṇayā*, *paṇeta*, *vāṇīḥ*, *kalyāṇī*, *kuṇapam*, *vāṇaḥ*, *śataśoṇāśruti*, *dhāṇikā*, *meṇī*. (12) *Avagraha* [is applied] to *vṛṣan*, *śīrṣan*, *brahman*, *kṣaṇ*, *carman*, and *carṣaṇ*. (13) *Ṛṇa*, *ṣaṇa*, *ṣṇam*, *ṇara*, and *āvṇa*—these are the *prākṛta* [forms]. (14) In *yuṣman*, when followed by *agni*, there is no elision (*alopa*) of the final *n* when followed by a stop (*sparśa*), except in the case of *anta*; this applies even when there is an intervening consonant (*vyavāya*), provided it is not *ś*, *s*, *c*, *ṭ*, *t*, or *v*. (15)
According to Pauṣkarasādi, the letter *ḷ* following a conjunct vowel becomes *ḍaṃ*; this is the view of Pauṣkarasādi. Thus ends the thirteenth chapter.
The fourteenth chapter begins.

Now begins the fourteenth chapter. 1. A consonant preceded by a vowel is a "two-syllable" (dvivarṇa) [word], provided that a consonant follows it. 2. According to Pauṣkarasādi, a stop-consonant (sparśa) preceded by the letter *l* is also [a two-syllable word]. 3. According to some teachers, it is a stop-consonant alone [that is so designated]. 4. [A consonant] following the letter *r* [is a two-syllable word]. 5. However, when the second or fourth [stop-consonants] are followed by a consonant, the preceding [vowel] is [part of the same syllable]. 6. And this is always the case when they are preceded by the letter *r*. 7. And also when preceded by the letter *l*. 8. This is the reading regarding prefixes (*upasarga*): [the rule applies] when *ati*, *ati-dhāma*, *parama*, and *bhūta* precede, as well as in the cases of *chakṣi* and *bhuje*. 9. A first [stop-consonant] following a voiceless sibilant (*ūṣman*) [is a two-syllable word].

9. For Bhinidhāna, [the *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya*] follow a *sparśa* (stop) that is followed by a semivowel (*sasthāna*). 10. According to Plākṣi, they follow a voiceless (*aghoṣa*) [consonant]. 11. According to the one named Plākṣāyaṇa, they follow an aspirated (*uttama*) [consonant]. 12. A first [stop] followed by a sibilant (*ūṣman*) becomes the second [stop of its class]. 13. According to Bāḍabhīkāra, [the *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya*] follow a non-homorganic (*asasthāna*) [consonant]. 14. Or rather, not so. 15. At the end of a word (*avasāna*), there are the *repha* (visarga), *visarjanīya*, *jihvāmūlīya*, and *upadhmānīya*. 16. A sibilant (*ūṣman*) followed by a vowel remains as it is. 17. According to Plākṣi and Plākṣāyaṇa, it remains when followed by a first [stop]. 18. According to Hārīta, a voiceless sibilant (*ūṣman*) [remains]. 19. And the letter *ha* [remains] when followed by the letter *ra*. 20. And the *ṭa*-class [remains] when followed by the *ta*-class.

21. The *la*-group [consonants] followed by the letter *ya* [are doubled]. 22. And [the same applies to a consonant] followed by another [consonant]. 23. [A consonant] followed by a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) or a member of its own group (*vargīya*) [is doubled]. 24. A non-final (non-uttama) [consonant] followed by a final (uttama) [consonant of its group is doubled]. 25. Now, according to some teachers: 26. The letter *la* followed by a *ha*, *śa*, or *va* [is doubled]. 27. A [consonant] followed by a stop (*sparśa*) [is doubled]. 28. And a word-final [consonant] followed by a consonant [is doubled] according to the Prākṛta rule. 29. An unraised vowel (*anudātta*) following a raised vowel (*udātta*) is circumflex (*svarita*). 30. This is true even when [the *udātta*] is separated by a consonant. 31. It is not so when followed by an *udātta* or a *svarita*. 32. Not [so], according to Āgniveśyāyana. 33. "All [rules] are not [binding]," say some; "all [rules] are not [binding]," say some. Thus ends the fourteenth chapter. The fifteenth chapter begins.

Now begins the fifteenth chapter. 1. When the letter *na* becomes *ra*, *ūṣman*, or *ya*, [the preceding vowel] is nasalized (*anunāsika*), provided that [the *na*] has been elided or its *m* has been dropped. 2. According to some teachers, it is not so. 3. In those cases, however, there is an *anusvāra*. 4. Also in the case of *srā?* and similar forms, when within a single word (*ekapada*) and followed by an *ūṣman*. 5. That which precedes a modification of a final *n* [is nasalized]. 6. According to some teachers, short vowels (*samānākṣara*) that are not *pragrahas* are nasalized. 7. And according to Śāṅkhāyana and Kāṇḍamāyana, a protracted (*pluta*) word is also [nasalized]. 8. But the vowel *a* remains [unchanged] even in *saṃhitā*, according to some teachers. 9. Not everything is subject to the same rule; for the former teachers, everything is subject to the same rule. Thus ends the fifteenth chapter. Now begins the sixteenth chapter.

Now begins the sixteenth chapter. Now follow those [words] preceded by *sa-*: 1. Words beginning with *sra*, *soha*, and *pāśa* [preserve their accent] when followed by a vowel. 2. Also when followed by a modified (*vikṛta*) vowel. 3. And that which is preceded by *rā*. 4. *Śaṃstān* [preserves its accent] when it is oxytone (acute on the final syllable). 5. *Aśaṃsan*. 6. Not so *śāsanam* when it occurs with *viśasanena*. 7. *Mā* at the beginning of a word is not grave (anudātta) when followed by a vowel. 8. That which is preceded by *pum* or *īp* always [preserves its accent]. 9. And also when followed by *sakāya*. 10. Not when preceded by an avagraha. 11. Also in the cases: *māsimāsu*, *māsomāsām*. 12. [The same applies to: *hi*, *pujigā*, *jighā*, *chaṃsine*, *ataṃsayat*, *ātāṃsīt*, *kanīyājyāyāḥ*.

*drāghīyān*, *raghīyān*, *śreyān*, *hasīyān*, *vasīyān*, *bhūyāṃsaḥ*, *ajakṣivat*, *ajaghnivat*, *ajigivat*, *ajīgivat*, *ātasthivat*, *ādāśvat*, *adīdivat*, *apibat*, *apīpivat*, *avidvat*, *aviśivat*, *aśuśruvat*, *asasravat*. (13) The vowels *ā*, *ī*, and *ū* [do not undergo elision] when followed by *si* or *parā* at the end of a word. (14) Even when modified [by a suffix], [the vowel remains]. (18) A short vowel that does not have the form *ā* [remains unchanged] before a form containing the letter *kṛ*. (16) In a word consisting of two syllables, [the vowel] is not always [unchanged] before a suffix beginning with a consonant. (17) Also [unchanged are the forms]: *ṛjīṣi*, *jigāsi*, *jighāsi*, *ajāsi*, *yajjāsi*, *dadāsi*, *dadhāsi*, and *vartayāsi*. (18)

19. *daṃsanābhyām*, *daṃsobhiḥ*, *daṃsam*, *vṛṣadaṃśaḥ*, *daṃśukāt*, *daṃṣṭrābhyām*, *paraḥ*. 20. *maṃsyai*, *amaṃsata*, *iyam*, *satyam*, *aṃsan*, *vaṃsate*, *vaṃsagaḥ*. 21. *unna vaṃśam*. 22. *akraṃsta*, *akraṃsyata*, *ariṃsyata*, *bhraṃśate*. 23. And [the suffix] *raṃhyai*. 24. The vowel *e* (aikāra) is the final element of the word *ukhya*. 25. The word *viritri* occurs in enumerations (*saṃkhyā*). 26. *śim̐śumāraḥ*, *śim̐ṣat*, *saṃśvāsam*, *saṃsrāsam*, *saṃsṛṣṭa*, *saṃkṛtya*, *sakṛm̐ta*, *saṃśita*, *saṃśatā*, *kiṃśilā*, *kiṃśilā*. 27. The root *sitṛdṛ* followed by the letter *ha*.

And in *maṃhiṣṭhasya* [28]: *ādir aṃhatiḥ*, *aṃho 'ṃhoḥ*, *aṃho 'mugati*, *aṃhā aṃhasaḥ*, *ahaṃsām aṃśam*, *aṃśubhir aṃśabhuvām*, *aṃśuśū aṃśavaḥ*, *aṃśur aṃśum*, *aṃśūn aṃśunā*, *aṃśor aṃśāya*, *upāṃśv aṃśau* [29]. There is an acute accent (*udātta*) on the *avagraha* in *aṃse*, *aṃsāya*, *aṃsābhyām*, and *aṃsau* [30]. *nāsāvā*, *nāsāvā* [31]. Thus ends the sixteenth chapter;
[now] the seventeenth chapter.

Now begins the seventeenth chapter. 1. Śaityāyana maintains that there is a stronger nasalization (*ānunāsikya*) in the case of the *anusvāra* before the final consonants. 2. Kauhalīputra holds that it is the same everywhere. 3. Bhāradvāja says that it is subtle (*aṇu*) in the case of the *anusvāra*. 4. The Elder Kauṇḍinya maintains that there is no *repha* (r-sound) for the vowel *ā*, because of its transformation into *ṣma* and *ya*; furthermore, when [the *anusvāra*] is elided, it is due to the elision of *m*, and each subsequent instance is stronger than the preceding one. 5. And here, the duration of the consonant is greater than that of the vowel. 6. According to Pauṣkarasādi, there is a more firm effort (*dṛḍhaprayatnatara*) in the case of the accent (*svara*) and the transition (*vikrama*).

"By means of a specific effort, one should [pronounce] all the phonemes," says Śaityāyana (7). "One should indicate the phonemes neither too clearly nor indistinctly; like a pot full of water being carried by a steady person, one should proceed according to one's ability," says Ātreya—Ātreya (8). Thus ends the seventeenth chapter.
The eighteenth chapter begins.

Now begins the eighteenth chapter. Some say that the syllable *oṃ* is the *praṇava*, consisting of two and a half morae (*mātrā*). (1) According to Śaityāyana, it consists of any one of the acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), or circumflex (*svarita*) accents. (2) According to Kauṇḍinya, it possesses a sustained, continuous tone (*pracaya*). (3) Its utterance is with a medium pitch (*madhyama*). (4) According to Plākṣi and Plākṣāyaṇa, it is circumflex (*svarita*). (5) According to Vālmīki, it is acute (*udātta*). (6) Or rather, all [these views] may be applied according to usage; indeed, all may be applied according to usage. (7) Thus ends the eighteenth chapter. Now begins the nineteenth chapter.

Now begins the nineteenth chapter. Where there is a low-pitched (nīca) vowel between two circumflex (svarita) vowels, or between two acute (udātta) vowels, or on either side of one of them, or between an acute and a circumflex vowel—that is the *vikrama*. (1) According to Kauṇḍinya, it is also preceded by a protracted (*pracaya*) vowel. (2) Some say it lasts for two *yamas*; others say it lasts for two *yamas* and is of the measure of an atom (*aṇumātra*). (3) In that very same original state (*prakṛti*). (4) Not in the previous treatise; not in the previous treatise. (5) Thus ends the nineteenth chapter. Now begins the twentieth chapter.

Now begins the twentieth chapter. 1. When the vowels *i* and *u* become *y* and *v*, [the resulting combination] is called *kṣaipra*, provided both are acute (*udātta*). 2. However, one should know that where a syllable containing *y* or *v* is accented while the word remains in its uncontracted form—whether preceded by an unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel or not—the rule applies invariably. 3. Furthermore, if the acute accent belongs to a syllable situated across two words (*nānāpada-stha*), yet it is pronounced according to the rules of *saṃhitā*, that is called *prātihata*. 4. From that [same cause], when the vowel *a* is elided, it is called *abhinihata*. 5. When *u* becomes *v*, it is called *praśliṣṭa*. 6. When there is a hiatus between words (*pada-vivṛtti*), it is called *pādavṛtta*. 7. That which is preceded by an acute vowel is called *tairovyañjana*. Thus [ends the section].

8. The names of the *svaras* [are as follows]. 9. In the case of *kṣaipra* and *nitya*, it is more firm (*dṛḍhatara*). 10. And in the case of *abhinihita*. 11. In the cases of *praśliṣṭa* and *prātihata*, it is softer (*mṛdutara*). 12. In the cases of *tairovyañjana* and *pādavṛtta*, it is increasingly lighter (*alpatara-alpatara*). Thus ends the twentieth chapter. The twenty-first chapter begins.

Now begins the twenty-first chapter. 1. A consonant (*vyañjana*) is a limb (*aṅga*) of a vowel (*svara*). 2. That [consonant] has the vowel following it as its own. 3. A [consonant] that has reached its end belongs to the preceding [vowel]. 4. [A consonant] at the beginning of a conjunct (*saṃyoga*) belongs to the preceding [vowel]. 5. And [a consonant] not joined (*asaṃhita*) with what follows belongs to the preceding [vowel]. 6. An *anusvāra* and a *svarabhakti* belong to the preceding [vowel]. 7. A nasalized semi-vowel (*anta-stha*) followed by a non-homogeneous [consonant] belongs to the preceding [vowel]. 8. [A nasalized semi-vowel] followed by a sibilant (*nāsikya*) belongs to the preceding [vowel]. 9. A contact consonant (*sparśa*) followed by a sibilant (*ūṣman*), provided the sibilant is the following one, belongs to the preceding [vowel]. 10. In a continuous text (*saṃhitā*), the accumulation (*pracaya*) of grave (*anudātta*) syllables following a circumflex (*svarita*) is heard as acute (*udātta*). 11. [This does not occur] when an acute or circumflex syllable follows. 12. After a contact consonant that is not the last of its class, when followed by the last [consonant] of its class, nasals (*nāsikya*) arise in their respective order.

13. When those [consonants] are being repeated, there is no nasalization after the letter *ha*. 14. There is nasalization (*anusvāra*) before a nasal consonant that follows a non-nasal. 15. In the combination of a *repha* (visarga) and a sibilant, there is a svarabhakti vowel attached to the *repha*. 16. This does not occur in the case of a *krama-pāṭha* when followed by a first-class (velar) consonant; nor when followed by a first-class consonant. Thus ends the twenty-first chapter. The twenty-second chapter begins.

Now begins the twenty-second chapter: Sound is the material cause of all phonemes (varṇas). 1. When there is a change in its form, there is a change in the phoneme. 2. In this regard, we shall provide examples of the substances of sound. 3. The particles *kāra* and *kāraḥ* are used as indicators (*nirdeśaka*). 4. The particle *ca* and also *api* are used as subsequent indicators (*anvādeśaka*). 5. The particles *tu*, *atha*, and *eva* are used as restrictors (*vinivartaka*), governing markers (*adhikāraka*), and determiners (*avadhāraka*). 6. The particle *vā* indicates an option (*vaibhāṣika*). 7. The particle *na* is a negator (*pratiṣedhaka*). 8. Expansion (*āyāma*), harshness (*dāruṇya*), and subtlety (*aṇutva*) of the internal space (*kha*) are the causes for making sounds high-pitched (*uccaiḥ*). 9. Relaxation (*anvavasarga*), softness (*mārdava*), and vastness (*urutā*) of the internal space are the causes for making sounds low-pitched (*nīcaiḥ*).

There are ten syllables (*karāṇi*), and there are three positions (*sthānāni*)—low (*mandra*), middle (*madhyama*), and high (*tāra*). In that regard, there are twenty-one types of pauses (*yamāḥ*): the pause at the end of a *ṛk*-verse, the pause at the end of a word (*padavirāmaḥ*), the pause at the end of a *vivṛtti*, the pause at the end of a *vivṛtti* within a single word, and [pauses] of three morae (*trimātra*), two morae, one mora, and half a mora, respectively. One should know that all those which end in a consonant, as well as long vowels, those preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), and likewise nasalized (*anunāsika*) ones, are heavy; the remaining ones, other than these, are light. That which does not end in a consonant...
"Understand that which is short and not followed by a conjunct consonant, and which is uncombined with an anusvāra—this is light; understand this as light. Thus ends the twenty-second chapter.
The twenty-third chapter begins.

Now begins the twenty-third chapter. Now, the specific production of phonemes (*varṇa*). 1. "From the secondary articulation (*anupradāna*), from the contact (*saṃsarga*), from the place of articulation (*sthāna*), and from the arrangement of the organs (*karaṇavinyāsa*), the distinction of phonemes arises; and the measure [of sound] arises from the fifth [factor]. 2. Sound (*śabda*) joined with phonemes is the origin of speech (*vāc*). 3. There are seven places of speech (*vācasthāna*). 4. These are: the whispered (*upāṃśu*), the resonant (*dhvāna*), the roaring (*nimada*), the sounding (*upabdimat*), the low (*mandra*), the middle (*madhyama*), and the high (*tāra*). 5. That which is accompanied by the organs of articulation but lacks audible sound and involves mental application is the whispered (*upāṃśu*). 6. The non-perception of vowels and consonants is the resonant (*dhvāna*). 7. The perception... [text breaks off]

8. Deafness is the loss of resonance. 9. "With sound" means accompanied by resonance (*upabdimat*). 10. Low (*mandra*) in the chest, middle (*madhyama*) in the throat, and high (*tāra*) in the head. 11. In each of these three places—low and so forth—there are seven *yamas* (consonant doubling). 12. [The seven notes are] the drawn-out (*kṛṣṭa*), first, second, third, fourth, low (*mandra*), and excessively high (*atisvārin*). 13. Their perception is like that of a flame. 14. The three—the second, first, and drawn-out—are the *āhlāraka* notes. 15. For the Taittirīyakas, there are four starting from the low (*mandra*) and ending with the second. 16. For the Taittirīyas, the low (*mandra*) follows the second.

The third and fourth [stages] immediately following that are called the "fourfold" (*caturyamam*). (16) Within that, there is an intermediate operation consisting of two *yamas*. (17) We shall explain that. (18) It has been stated that this is the "fourfold. (19) One should recite it with the sequence and non-sequence perfected, neither too fast nor too slow, endowed with the natural accents of low and high pitch; one should recite it firmly and evenly—firmly and evenly. (20) Thus ends the twenty-third chapter. The twenty-fourth chapter begins.

Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter. Now, the four types of *saṃhitā*: (1) *pada-saṃhitā*, (2) *akṣara-saṃhitā*, (3) *varṇa-saṃhitā*, and (4) *aṅga-saṃhitā*. The conjunction of various words through their coalescence is designated as *pada-saṃhitā*. Just as with *pada-saṃhitā*, the same applies to *akṣara-saṃhitā* and the others. [The phonetic qualities include: heaviness (*gurutva*), lightness (*laghutā*), evenness (*sāmya*), short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*) vowels; elision (*lopa*), augmentation (*āgama*), and modification (*vikāra*); the natural state (*prakṛti*), displacement (*vikrama*), and sequential order (*krama*); the circumflex (*svarita*), acute (*udātta*), and grave (*nīca*) accents; breath (*śvāsa*), resonance (*nāda*), and indeed the bodily articulation (*aṅga*).

All of this, however, must be understood by one studying the Chāndas language. One who knows the distinctions of the *pada* and *krama* [recitations], who is skilled in the sequence of phonemes (*varṇa-krama*), and who knows the divisions of accents and prosodic measures (*mātrā*), may enter the assembly of teachers—may enter the assembly of teachers. Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter; the Taittirīya Prātiśākhya is complete.
